1:
The scene is Esther's second banquet, and the witnesses set the table before they weigh a word. The reformed John Gill notes that the king and Haman came “to drink” — to partake of the banquet of wine the queen had spread, and came in answer to the invitation she had given them, the very phrase the next verse will name outright at v.2. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the clause with the same care: the two men came “to drink,” to share the banquet in the queen's own apartment. And they set this feast in the frame of the whole chapter — following the first banquet at Esther 5:6, it is the ground on which the reversal now turns: here the king will inquire once more, here Esther will at last unburden the plea she has twice held back, and here the favourite's ruin will break over him before the wine is done.

It is the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry who catches the temperature of the moment in a single stroke: “the king in humour, and Haman out of humour, meet at Esther's table.” The one comes relaxed and expansive, glad still of his queen's company and eager to learn her desire; the other comes inwardly galled, brought low the very morning before, when he had been made to lead through the streets in honour the man he most wished to destroy. Neither yet knows what the table holds. The king does not suspect that the petition he keeps pressing touches his own decree and the life of the woman beside him; Haman does not dream that the queen who has twice singled him out for so intimate a feast has singled him out to be arraigned.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very plainness of the verse becomes a kind of suspense. Twice already Esther has kept her petition in reserve, waiting for a surer hour, and now that hour has come. The banquet Haman had paraded to his friends as the crown of his fortunes is the appointed place of his undoing; and the reader, who knows what the actors cannot, watches a proud man take his seat at a table set, unknown to him, for judgment. So the three witnesses converge to open the chapter where the last one closed — a king in good humour, a favourite in false security, and a queen about to speak the words that will turn the feast into a tribunal.
2:
The king renews his question — “What is thy petition, queen Esther? and it shall be granted thee” — and the witnesses hear in the repetition both a royal eagerness and a hidden hand. The reformed John Gill counts it the third time the king has pressed the question, and reads the persistence as more than curiosity: it was of God that the matter was kept upon the king's mind and that he was moved to solicit her plea, for otherwise it would not have been easy for Esther to introduce so grave a suit herself. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the same providence in the king's memory: had he now forgotten that Esther had an errand, and not asked again, she could scarcely have known how to renew it; but he was mindful of it, and stood “bound with the threefold cord of a promise thrice made” to favour her.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the setting and the sense. Keil and Delitzsch note that the king asked again on the second day just as he had done on the first at Esther 5:6, renewing his lavish pledge that her request should be performed “even to the half of the kingdom”; and only now does Esther take courage to speak, the request framed, they observe, as the very price she offers, her life and her people's set against the king's bounty. Charles Ellicott hears in the renewed question the king's own shrewd assumption — that Esther's invitations to her banquets were never her real errand, but merely prepared the way for it — so that he presses her to name at last the thing she has so carefully approached.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds a blunter, more human note, following the Vulgate's postquam vino incaluerat: it was after the king had been warmed with wine that the question came, and in such a mood he was the more likely to fall in with the queen's measures. The witnesses do not divide; they gather around a single scene in which every circumstance conspires for Esther — the king's good humour, the mellowing wine, the thrice-repeated pledge, the very forgetfulness that might have sunk her suit turned instead into a persistent invitation. What Ellicott traces to the king's shrewdness and Clarke to the wine, Gill and Henry trace higher still, to the God who holds the heart of the king and now bends it, at the appointed hour, toward the deliverance of his people.
3:
No sooner is she pressed than Esther makes her venture, and the witnesses linger over the courage and the quiet devotion behind her first words. The reformed John Gill pictures the manner of it: not, as one account would have it, flinging herself at the king's knees, but rather — as the Targum suggests — lifting her eyes to heaven and putting up a secret ejaculation for direction and success before she spoke. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that she opens with the same deferential formula she had used at Esther 5:8 — “If I have found favour in thy sight, O king” — and then, at last, brings out the petition she has twice withheld: “Let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request.”

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses admire the art of the appeal. Adam Clarke judges it “very artfully, as well as very honestly, managed,” framed to strike straight at the king's affections: what — is the life of the queen he tenderly loves in any kind of danger? John Wesley reads her plea as the barest of requests — “it is my only request, that thou wouldst not give me up to the malice of that man” — and joins the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry in feeling its pathos. Even a stranger, even a condemned criminal, both observe, is permitted to petition for his life; but that a friend, a wife, a queen should be driven to beg for her own is a thing deeply affecting.

Henry draws out what makes the two lives she pleads for so precious that no time should be lost in saving them: majesty and multitude. If it is a crowned head that is struck at, it is time to stir — “Let my life be given me”; and if it is not one life or two but a whole people, and a people dear to her, that are aimed at, then no pains should be spared to prevent the mischief. The witnesses do not divide. They show a queen who has prayed before she pleads, who couches a matter of state in the tenderest personal terms, and who stakes everything on the king's love — asking first, and most movingly, not for her nation in the abstract but for her own imperilled life, that the king's heart, once engaged for her, might be enlarged to spare the rest. The majesty of the person struck at and the multitude of the innocent doomed with her are, on Henry's reading, the two pleas that together will not let a just prince keep silent.
4:
Now Esther lays the charge bare — “we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish” — and the witnesses note first how deliberately she borrows the language of the death-warrant itself. The reformed John Gill hears in her piled-up verbs an echo of the very decree, and in “we are sold” a pointed allusion to the ten thousand talents Haman had offered to buy their ruin. Charles Ellicott, reading as a grammatical-historical witness, confirms that the words are “the identical words used in the king's proclamation” for the Jews' destruction at Esther 3:13, and marks how much she risks in speaking them: with this sentence Esther at once confesses her nationality and stakes the fate of herself and her race on the momentary impulse of a fickle lord — grounds that might at any other time have proved untrustworthy, but which God has willed shall now suffice, for the hearts of kings are in his rule and governance.

Over the verse's obscure last clause — “although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage” — the witnesses genuinely differ, and Ellicott sets the crux out plainly. It may mean, he says, either that Haman, for all his willingness to pour silver into the treasury, cannot make up for the loss the king must suffer by a wholesale massacre in his realm; or that, had the Jews been merely sold into slavery rather than slaughtered, Esther would have held her peace, the affliction not being worth troubling the king about. Ellicott prefers the former, and the wesleyan-arminian voices stand with him: Adam Clarke insists that not even ten thousand talents could compensate the state for the loss of a whole nation throughout its generations, and John Wesley reckons the damage in the customs and tributes the king yearly receives from the Jews, which Haman's payment could never repair.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives voice to the other sense: had they been sold into bondage she would not have complained, for in time they might have recovered their liberty; it is because they are sold “to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish” that it is time to speak. To persecute an industrious and peaceable people, Henry adds, is as impolitic as it is impious, weakening and impoverishing the very prince who allows it. The witnesses converge on the force of the plea even while they part on its grammar. Whether the clause weighs a massacre's cost against a bribe or contrasts slaughter with mere servitude, all agree that Esther has framed her appeal to touch the king in a tender place — pity for herself, and the plain interest of his own crown — and so to bring him to relent.
5:
The king's reply bursts out in broken, agitated speech, and the witnesses read his very grammar as the register of his rage. The reformed John Gill dwells on the doubled verb of the Hebrew — “and the King Ahasuerus said, and he said” — which he takes not, with Jarchi, to mean the king now spoke to her directly as royal kin, but to express the ruffle of his mind, the wrath that made him say it over and over with a stern countenance. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke renders the tumbling original almost word for word — “Who? He? This one? And where? This one? He? Who hath filled his heart to do thus?” — and finds in its confusion a man struck to the core by the horrible nature of a plot so cruel and diabolical. John Wesley likewise hears expressions “short and doubled, as proceeding from a discomposed and enraged mind,” the king astonished that anyone should dare so to circumvent him as to imperil his own queen along with his innocent subjects.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the same agitation and then to its root. The repetition of the verb, they note, betrays the king's excited indignation as he asks who it is “whom his heart hath filled” to do such a thing; for evil thoughts proceed from the heart and fill the man and drive him to evil deeds, a truth they anchor in Matthew 15:19 and Ecclesiastes 8:11.

But the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and Wesley together press the sharpest irony of the scene. The king stands amazed at a wickedness he himself is chargeable with; for it was Ahasuerus who consented to the bloody edict against the Jews, sealing it with his own ring, so that Esther, had she chosen, might too truly have turned his own outburst upon him: “Thou art the man.” We sometimes startle, Henry observes, at the mention of that very evil we ourselves have had a hand in. Henry marvels on two counts — that any heart should be so bad as to devise such a thing, for surely Satan had filled it, and that any should be so bold as to dare it. The witnesses do not divide. They show a despot genuinely horrified at a crime he had authorized without a thought, his fury real and yet self-condemning; and they leave the reader to feel the justice of it, that the king's indignation at Haman is, unknown to himself, a verdict upon his own careless cruelty.
6:
Asked who the man is, Esther does not flinch: “The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman.” The reformed John Gill weighs the charge she levels to his face. Haman was an enemy not only to her and her people but an adversary to the king himself, having drawn him into a measure ruinous to his revenue and his reputation; and by naming him openly, in his hearing, Esther gave him his just character and yet left him — could he have done it — the opportunity to clear himself. The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the sudden collapse of the favourite. Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott both render the word for Haman's terror as a shrinking back in dread — the same verb used at Daniel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 21:30 — as the man who a moment before had reclined in honour now cowers before the king and the queen.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gather around Haman's fear and find it richly deserved. It was time for him to fear, they say almost in one voice, when the queen was his prosecutor, the king his judge, and his own conscience a witness against him; and the surprising turns of providence that very morning — his forced parade of Mordecai through the streets — could only sharpen his dread. Henry adds that Haman is now “cast into a net by his own feet,” the schemer entangled in the snare he laid, finding himself in straits at the very hour he thought himself in the fulness of his sufficiency. The invitation he had lately paraded before his friends as the crown of his honour has become, in a moment, the occasion of his terror.

Henry lingers, too, on the boldness of Esther's accusation. She charges Haman before his face, for to that end he was invited; it is he, she declares, who designed their murder and, worse, basely drew the king in to be an unwitting partner in the crime. The witnesses do not divide. They show a queen who has chosen her ground with care — the accused seated at her own table, the king within earshot, every avenue of escape already closed — and a favourite whose glittering security dissolves in an instant into naked fear. What Haman had built with patience and pride comes down at a single sentence from the woman he had never troubled to suspect, and the reader sees the whole weight of the book's peril begin, here, to swing back upon its author.
7:
The king cannot contain himself; he rises in wrath and strides out into the palace garden, and the witnesses follow both his fury and the collapse of the man he leaves behind. The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley read the withdrawal alike: the king could not bear the sight of Haman, and went out both to let his passion cool and to consider what punishment so great a treachery deserved; his going, Wesley adds, showed the violent commotion of his mind. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the pregnant Hebrew — the king “arose” from the banquet straight into the garden — while Haman remained behind to beg for his life, “for he saw that there was evil determined against him,” the word for that doom meaning a thing already completed and fixed, as at 1 Samuel 20:7; Charles Ellicott glosses the same phrase tightly, “the evil, the doom,” for Haman now knew he had no mercy to expect from the king unless the queen should intercede.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the fullest portrait. The king, he suggests, did not summon his wise counsellors, being ashamed to consult them about undoing what he had so rashly done without them; he walked in the garden vexed at himself, that he should have been fool enough to doom a guiltless nation, and his own queen among them, on the base suggestions of a self-seeking man, and vexed at Haman, whom he had carried in his bosom and who had so abused his trust. Those who act with self-will, Henry observes, reflect upon it afterward with self-reproach; and when we are angry we should pause, as men who have rule over their own spirits, before we resolve.

But Henry's deeper interest is the great reversal now visible in the room. See how mean Haman looks, standing up first and then falling down at Esther's feet to beg for the life he had schemed to take, and to offer all he had — for the most haughty and imperious in their prosperity are commonly the most abject when the wheel turns. And see how great Esther looks, she who of late was doomed to the slaughter like a sheep, now with her sworn enemy at her mercy. In this Henry hears the note of the Magnificat: God regards the low estate of his handmaiden and scatters the proud in the imagination of their hearts, as Mary sang in Luke 1:51; and he sets beside it the promise to Philadelphia, that God would make the synagogue of Satan come and worship before the feet of his beloved in Revelation 3:9. The day is coming, Henry says, when those who hate and persecute God's chosen ones will gladly be beholden to them. The witnesses converge: a king storming in the garden, a favourite grovelling at a Jewish queen's feet, and over it all the quiet justice of a God who lifts the low and brings the proud man down.
8:
The king returns, and what he sees in the instant of his return seals Haman's fate. The reformed John Gill notes only that he came back a little cooler and more composed; but the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the fatal tableau: the king found Haman “fallen” upon the couch where Esther sat, collapsed as a suppliant at her very feet, and — crediting the man in his heat with the worst of designs — cried out, “Will he force the queen also before me in the house?” The verb, they note, means to tread under foot or subdue, here stretched to the sense of offering violence; and without waiting for any explanation the king, more infuriated still, passes upon Haman the sentence of death.

On one point the witnesses stand entirely together: the king did not truly believe that Haman meant to assault the queen. Adam Clarke says he must have known that in such circumstances the thought could not possibly exist; Charles Ellicott, that Ahasuerus knew perfectly well Haman's posture was that of a suppliant, his words being only the outlet of his anger; John Wesley, that he speaks “not out of real jealousy, but from an exasperated mind, which takes all occasions to vent itself against the person who gave the provocation”; and Matthew Henry, that the king had no such suspicion in earnest, but, musing on Haman's design against the queen's life and finding him in this posture, seized the occasion to loose his passion. What Haman intended for mercy is now, like everything he does, construed to his ruin.

Over the covering of Haman's face the witnesses supply the custom that explains it. The wesleyan-arminian Wesley reads it as the servants shielding the king from the sight of a man he now loathed, and as the mark set upon a condemned person, whose face was covered; Clarke draws the Roman parallel exactly, the judge delivering the criminal to the lictor with the words, “Go, serjeant; cover his head, and hang him on the accursed tree”; Ellicott adds that the man must never see the king's face again, pointing back to the counsellors who “saw the king's face” in Esther 1:13. Ellicott alone pauses to weigh the king himself, and will not gild him: base and worthless as Ahasuerus is — the very massacre had gone out with his full knowledge and consent, though he now ignores his own share in it — God has made him for the moment the blind instrument of a deliverance he never intended, as great ends are sometimes wrought by unholy hands. The witnesses do not divide. They show a doom pronounced almost without words, a favourite's face veiled for execution, and a king whose righteous-seeming fury is itself half pretext — yet bent, all unknowing, to the saving of the people he had signed away.
9:
With the king's wrath at its height, one of his eunuchs turns it toward the very instrument of Haman's malice. The reformed John Gill identifies the speaker as Harbonah, one of the seven chamberlains, whom Josephus calls Sabouchadas. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that Harbonah, already named at Esther 1:10, points to the gallows “also” — the little word betraying that the other eunuchs had already been laying particulars of Haman's crime before the king — and recall that Mordecai, for whom the tree was raised, had once “spoken good for the king” by disclosing the plot against his life at Esther 2:22. On that same tree the king orders Haman hanged, and it is done without delay. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the courtiers' swift change of wind: the very chamberlain lately sent to fetch Haman to the banquet now informs against him, and now that Mordecai is the favourite, everything is remembered that may fill up the measure of Haman's iniquity — so little can proud men count on the interest they think they hold.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the moment into a meditation on retribution. “Harm watch, harm catch,” he says; and he recalls Perillus, the first man burnt alive in the brazen bull he had forged for the torture of others, sealing the point with the poet's line — there can be no juster law than that the contrivers of death should perish by their own invention. The gallows Haman built to overtop the city and shame Mordecai becomes the beam of his own hanging.

Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, hears the climax of the whole book in the pithy words that follow — they hanged Haman on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai — and marks that it stood at his own house, so that he met his fate in sight of the children and servants and the wife who had given him such cold comfort. Thus, Ellicott says, God not only delivers his people but brings upon the enemy the very destruction he had devised, for “he hath fallen himself into the pit that he digged for other”; and he reads in Haman's discomfiture a figure of a greater victory, the Saviour treading down the foe too mighty for us, a type of the triumph of the Lamb over sin and Satan. The witnesses do not divide; from the eunuch's disclosure to the poet's maxim they trace one lesson — that the snare set for the innocent closes, by a righteous providence, upon the head that set it.
10:
The sentence is carried out in a single breath — “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” — and the witnesses close the chapter on the justice of it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the bare fact and its effect without comment: Haman is hanged, and then was the king's wrath pacified. The reformed John Gill lingers only over the place. Not within the house, he thinks, but more probably in Haman's own courtyard, in the sight of his family and friends — or else the gallows was carried out and set up beyond the city, for the apocryphal supplement to the book says he was hanged at the gates of Susa, with all his household, God speedily rendering him vengeance according to his deserts.

It is the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry who reads the execution as a sermon in three heads. Here is pride brought down: the man who expected everyone to do him homage is made an ignominious spectacle to the world, for God resists the proud, and those whom he resists find him irresistible. Here is persecution punished: Haman was a wicked man on many counts, but his enmity to God's church was his most provoking crime, and for that the God to whom vengeance belongs here reckons with him. And here is mischief returned upon its own contriver, the wicked snared in the work of his own hands, as the Psalms so often promise in Psalm 7:15-16. Haman is justly hanged on the very gallows he had unjustly reared; had he never built it, Henry remarks, perhaps the king would never have thought of hanging him at all.

Henry sets the day's reversal in a single line: in the morning Haman was designing the royal robes for himself and the gallows for Mordecai, but the tables are turned, and now Mordecai has the crown and Haman the cross — the Lord is known by such judgments, as it is written in Proverbs 11:8. The sentence was short and the execution speedy, and no man asked what Haman had to say why it should not be done. The witnesses do not divide. They leave the chapter where pride always tends, with the enemy of God's people fallen into his own pit and a king's anger stilled at last — not by any innocence in the man he condemned, but by the working of a justice that turns the persecutor's craft back upon his own neck.
